papers.title: Cardiomyocyte-Derived Cell-Free DNA in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
papers.abstract: The hearts of patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) are exposed to chronic wall stress and subclinical myocardial injury, yet conventional biomarkers such as cardiac troponin lack specificity for cardiomyocyte death. Here we evaluate whether cardiomyocyte-derived cell-free DNA (cfDNA-CM), quantified by whole-genome bisulfite sequencing and methylation-based cell-type deconvolution, can be measured in clinically stable HCM. We analyze 57 plasma samples from patients with HCM and 10 from patients with acute myocardial infarction as positive controls. Control samples show higher total cfDNA yield and cfDNA-CM fractions than HCM samples, supporting assay validity. In HCM, cfDNA-CM ranges from 0% to 6.4% of total cfDNA; higher cfDNA-CM is associated with higher body mass index, obesity and obstructive sleep apnea, but not with NT-proBNP or high-sensitivity troponin I. Quantifying cfDNA-CM in stable HCM is feasible, and its association with cardiometabolic burden independent of traditional biomarkers suggests that cfDNA-CM reflects a distinct domain of myocardial injury and remodeling.

papers.title: Ordinal Probit Modeling of Loneliness, Relationship Difficulty, Worthlessness, and Depression in Midlife: An Ordinal Association Analysis of Psychosocial and Demographic Predictors
papers.abstract: Midlife is a time of significant social, economic, and health change, and the covariation between demographic and psychosocial characteristics and ill-being has both preventional and organisational implications. This is an attempt to produce a single ordinal variable summarising information about mental health- ill-being, and its dependence on demographic predictors. We measure mental ill-being through four midlife-related outcomes: loneliness frequency (RA1SA20G), ability to sustain close relationships (RA1SF1J), worthlessness frequency (RA1SA20F), and degree of depressive symptomatology (RA1PDEPRE), and explore a fifth, anxiety (RA1PANXIE) at the descriptive, but not inferential, level. The predictors are age and sex, pain of financial difficulty in meeting the monthly bills, purposefulness/agentic engagement, self-efficacy, sleep difficulty, contact with social media, meditation/relaxation use, and leisure vigorous activity. After removing missing or refused values (listwise deletion), 2,423 respondents (52.9% female; age range 23 to 76, mean 51.84, SD 14.20) from the initial 3,577 sample extract remain; we give univariate, one-variable summaries, merge sparse categories of the predictor variables through a limited number of theoretically motivated recodes, and establish the strength of association of predictor pairs with ordinal correlation coefficients (Kendall's tau-b, Stuart's tau-c, and rank-biserial correlation for sex). We fit maximum-likelihood ordinal probit models both as models with a sole predictor variable (each in turn) and as a conditional (multi-predictor) model with four predictors (bins of age, bill difficulty, purposefulness/agency, and sleep difficulty) as a function of cross-validated predictive accuracy estimates from stratified five-fold cross-validation. We find high cross-validated predictive accuracy for depression (0.864), and worthlessness (0.808), and lower but still modest predictive accuracy for loneliness (0.653 to 0.655) and the ability to sustain close relationships (0.291 to 0.304); single-predictor accuracy estimates were not improved substantially in the combined models. We discuss how our decisions about recode levels, the interpretation of the ordinal association coefficients, potential limitations of the models and how future predictions could benefit from the inclusion of sample weights, ordinal-loss functions for model assessment, ordinal proportional-odds diagnostics, and model-based causal pathways from longitudinal waves of the MIDUS study.

papers.title: Multicentre electrophysiology reveals the limits of auditory prediction responses as biomarkers of chronic tinnitus
papers.abstract: Identifying reliable neural biomarkers of chronic tinnitus remains challenging because ageing and hearing loss independently influence auditory cortical activity. Here, we investigated auditory expectation processing in 440 adults with (n = 226) and without (n = 214) chronic tinnitus using electroencephalography during a local-global auditory paradigm across six centres. Although several electrophysiological group differences emerged in unadjusted analyses, most were substantially attenuated after adjustment for demographic and audiological factors. Two clusters remained significant within the unexpected-omission-versus-sound contrast (44 to 100 ms and 356 to 476 ms), but neither survived correction across eight contrasts. Direct comparisons between expected and unexpected omissions revealed no significant group differences. Exploratory classification using selected EEG features achieved a cross-validated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.624, increasing to 0.689 when combined with demographic and audiological predictors. However, this improvement was not reproduced in held-out validation, and EEG features showed limited predictive value for tinnitus burden or loudness. These findings highlight a fundamental distinction between electrophysiological group differences and clinically informative individual-level biomarkers, underscoring the importance of controlling for confounding factors and establishing independent predictive validity in tinnitus research.

papers.title: Chronobiology of anthracycline cardiotoxicity across two biobanks
papers.abstract: Background. Anthracyclines are widely used chemotherapeutics limited by dose-dependent cardiotoxicity. Because cardiovascular physiology and drug handling oscillate across the day, the timing of drug administration may influence cardiac risk. Optimal timing may depend on both an individual's internal circadian phase and environmental light exposure. We tested whether dosing time is associated with anthracycline cardiotoxicity, whether this is also true of overall treatment outcomes, and whether optimal dosing time is modified by photoperiod and the genetically predicted chronotype. Methods. We analyzed ejection fraction (EF) change following anthracycline exposure in the All of Us research program (AoU; 70 patients) and incident heart failure (HF) in the Penn Medicine Biobank (PMBB; 843 patients). Dosing time was modeled on both clock-time and solar (time-from-sunrise) axes using flexible splines, with likelihood-ratio tests (LRT) for association and for interaction with photoperiod and a germline chronotype polygenic score (cPGS). The cPGS was validated against wearable-derived midsleep and heart-rate rhythms. Results. Dosing time was associated with anthracycline cardiotoxicity in both cohorts, with greater harm at later dosing times (AoU EF LRT p=0.011 clock, p=0.029 sunrise; PMBB HF p=0.052 sunrise, p=0.084 clock). No association was observed with non-HF mortality (p=0.75, 0.77), consistent with a narrowing of the therapeutic index. Photoperiod modified the dosing-time association (AoU p=0.064 clock, p=0.062 sunrise; PMBB p=0.023 clock, p=0.093 sunrise). Modification by cPGS was directionally consistent across cohorts but did not reach significance, likely reflecting attenuation of a polygenic proxy capturing limited chronotype variance. Conclusions. Anthracycline dosing time is associated with cardiotoxicity but not mortality and is modified by photoperiod, identifying dosing time as a modifiable, circadian-sensitive factor. These findings motivate prospective, chronotype- and season-informed studies of anthracycline scheduling.

papers.title: Scalp EEG seizure warning in children under a pre-specified, locked evaluation: confound audit, structured chance levels and a negative result
papers.abstract: Objective. Reported performance of scalp electroencephalographic (EEG) seizure prediction is often inflated by lenient evaluation and by the vigilance-state, clock-time and admission-trend structure of monitoring data. We asked how much short-horizon warning survives a pre-specified, locked evaluation. Approach. Continuous video-EEG from 21 monitored children (1315 h) formed the development cohort. A statistical-process-control warning method was evaluated under a written protocol, then re-designed as a state-conditioned, directional scheme on seven global EEG features, frozen with a hash-recorded configuration and time-stamped pre-specification, assessed by nested leave-one-patient-out cross-validation, and applied once to two validation cohorts (a second batch from the same unit and the public CHB-MIT database from Children's Hospital Boston; 101 evaluable seizures). Main results. The original method detected 44% of evaluable seizures at 0.48 false alarms per hour, no better than a random predictor (51%, p = 0.86); its statistic moved three times more with vigilance state than with seizure approach. The frozen scheme detected 15 of 45 development seizures (33%) at 0.47 false alarms per hour, above analytic (21%, p = 0.034) and permutation chance, but a predictor using only clock time, vigilance state and days since admission reproduced most of this, and the signal was confined to the last 30 min. In validation it detected 19 seizures (19%) at 0.60 false alarms per hour against 26% chance (p = 0.96); no secondary endpoint was met, and with the child as the unit of analysis no cohort was above chance. Significance. Vigilance state, clock time and admission trend inflate apparent warning performance unless the chance model preserves that structure, and the short-horizon signal did not generalise beyond its development cohort. Scalp-EEG warning should be evaluated under pre-specified rules against structured chance levels; the frozen scheme and framework are offered as a reference.

papers.title: Causal Emergence of Macroscopic Stochastic Dynamics from a Multi-modal Foundation Model of Human Sleep
papers.abstract: Sleep is an essential, self organizing physiological state conserved across species, yet its macroscopic coordination remains governed by unknown physical principles. For nearly sixty years, clinical medicine has classified sleep into heuristic, discrete 30 second epochs, an empirical convention that flattens continuous non-equilibrium dynamics and leaves deep subcortical neuromodulatory control fundamentally unobservable. Although emerging artificial intelligence foundation models can decode multimodal physiology with high accuracy, their high-dimensional representations remain uninterpretable black boxes, leaving the generative laws of sleep unformulated. Here we show that, across four independent multinational cohorts, causal emergence analysis of a multimodal foundation model condenses human sleep into a single continuous order parameter whose dynamics are well described by a Landau Ginzburg jump diffusion equation. This trajectory is physiologically structured: its overnight variance follows an AASM stage hierarchy (Wake, NREM, REM), and its diffusion shape tracks apnea hypopnea severity. Bidirectional clinical perturbations further support the decomposition: continuous positive airway pressure lowers baseline diffusion and apnea band spectral excess while shallowing the late-night potential well, whereas GABAergic agonism reduces the true jump rate and nocturnal awakenings without deepening the well. Length matched comparisons under dexmedetomidine sedation deepen the well and suppress jumps relative to natural sleep. By replacing empirical classification with an explicit stochastic description, our work uses a foundation model as a probe of physiological dynamics rather than only as a predictor and treats human sleep as an analytically tractable physical system. More broadly, the finding that multi-organ coordination during sleep can be summarized by a low dimensional order parameter suggests a general route from opaque artificial intelligence representations to testable macroscopic models of the subcortical dynamics that sustain human consciousness and fail in neuropsychiatric disease.

papers.title: Prenatal exposure to semi-volatile organic compounds and early childhood sleep duration
papers.abstract: Background: Adequate sleep duration is critical for early childhood development; however, environmental determinants of sleep during this period remain understudied. Objective: We evaluated associations between prenatal exposure to semi-volatile organic compounds (SVOCs) and parent-reported sleep duration among 147 children 2-24 months of age. Methods: Mothers in Project HOPE 1000, a prospective pregnancy cohort in central North Carolina, wore silicone wristbands for 5 days during each trimester, and 117 SVOCs were quantified. Generalized linear mixed-effects models were adjusted for child age, race, ethnicity, and an exposure-age interaction term. Results: At least 70% of wristbands had detectable levels of 36 SVOCs. Among 2-month-olds, higher prenatal exposure to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, phthalates, and organophosphate esters was associated with decreased sleep duration across daytime, nighttime, and total sleep over a 24-hour period (e.g., benzyl butyl phthalate exposure was associated with lower expected nighttime sleep duration (Multiplicative Change: 0.77, 95% Confidence Interval: 0.61, 0.95). Results among 2-month-olds were similar when exposure was assessed as a mixture. Associations were largely null at older ages across all sleep outcomes. Significance: Prenatal SVOC exposure may have significant impacts on sleep duration during early infancy. Future studies should assess how these differences relate to broader measures of sleep health.

papers.title: Sleepless nights: Caregiver burden among DLB patients with nighttime behaviors in the PACE-DLB Cohort
papers.abstract: Background Nighttime behaviors in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) may increase caregiver burden by disrupting sleep and respite. Objective To examine associations between nighttime-behavior severity, caregiver burden, caregiving time, and caregiver well-being in moderate-to-advanced DLB. Methods We analyzed baseline data from 188 patient-caregiver dyads in the multicenter PACE-DLB cohort. Nighttime behaviors were categorized as mild/absent or moderate/severe using the Neuropsychiatric Inventory Questionnaire. Caregiver burden was assessed using the shortened Zarit Burden Interview (sZBI). Secondary outcomes included caregiving time and well-being. Group comparisons and exploratory multivariable regression were performed. Results Moderate-to-severe nighttime behaviors were reported in 117 individuals (62.2%). Caregivers in this group reported more hours on duty daily (median 24 [IQR 15-24] vs 13 [6-24]; p=0.004), more time in the same room (6 vs 3 hours/day; p=0.011), and greater burden (median sZBI 21 [13-26] vs 18 [12-21]; p=0.015). Exploratory comparisons identified differences in prioritizing care recipients' needs (p=0.046) and caregiver sleep disruption (p=0.010). After adjustment for other neuropsychiatric symptoms and patient characteristics, the nighttime-behavior association was attenuated (beta=1.5, 95% CI -0.93 to 3.9; p=0.20), whereas anxiety remained associated with greater burden (beta=3.5, 95% CI 1.2-5.9; p=0.004). Conclusions Nighttime behaviors were associated with greater caregiver burden and caregiving demands in unadjusted analyses. Although the adjusted burden association was attenuated, nighttime behaviors may impose distinct challenges through increased supervision and disrupted caregiver sleep. Further studies are needed to determine whether interventions targeting nighttime behaviors can reduce caregiving burden.

papers.title: Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Acoziborole Supplements Clinical Drug-Drug Interaction Data and Predicts Time-dependent Interaction Duration Following Single-Dose Oral Treatment for African Sleeping Sickness
papers.abstract: Acoziborole is a novel single-dose oral treatment for gambiense human African trypanosomiasis (g-HAT). Acoziborole's long half-life and complex, time-dependent effects on drug-metabolizing enzymes necessitate drug-drug interaction (DDI) assessment. A physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model was developed to characterize acoziborole DDI potential in African patients with g-HAT and support product labeling recommendations. Model development used available physicochemical, in vitro binding and interaction parameters, and clinical pharmacokinetic data from healthy participants and participants with g-HAT. Clinical DDI data for cytochrome P450 (CYP) 3A4 and CYP2D6 substrates were used to assess and refine the PBPK model. Predicted PK was validated using independent clinical datasets. The model was applied to predict clinically untested scenarios, including time-dependent DDI with CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 probe substrates, and DDIs with CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, and BCRP substrates. The model adequately described acoziborole PK in healthy participants and participants with g-HAT. Simulations predicted strong CYP3A4 induction to ~4 weeks, then moderate to ~9 weeks and CYP2D6 clinically relevant inhibition for up to 3 months post-acoziborole administration. Clinically relevant exposure reductions were predicted for concomitantly administered CYP3A4 substrates, particularly during the first month post-acoziborole. Prolonged and clinically relevant exposure increases in sensitive CYP2D6 substrates were predicted, although DDI risk was lower and shorter for CYP2D6 substrates also metabolized by CYP3A4. Simulated interactions with other enzymes were weak-to-moderate, with minimal transporter-mediated effects. The findings supported discussions with regulatory agencies to inform duration-based risk management strategies and prescribing information for acoziborole, and co-administration with common medications in the target population.
